item.title: A Russian Bribe the Size of Europe

item.title: The Economic Toll of Israel’s Wars
item.dc:creator: Joseph Zeira
item.description: Israel’s economy may look strong, but three years of war have inflicted far greater damage than its robust stock market and appreciating currency suggest. Defense spending and government borrowing have risen sharply, while falling output and investment point to a prolonged recession.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Olympia de Maismont/AFP via Getty Images

Israel’s economy may look strong, but three years of war have inflicted far greater damage than its robust stock market and appreciating currency suggest. Defense spending and government borrowing have risen sharply, while falling output and investment point to a prolonged recession.

By Joseph Zeira

JERUSALEM—Israel’s election results make weeks of political negotiation all but certain. What is equally clear is that whatever government eventually takes office will need to begin reckoning with the mounting costs of Israel’s ongoing wars.

item.title: Rebalancing Nature’s Books
item.dc:creator: Homi Kharas, Julie McCarthy and Ichiro Sato
item.description: The first report card on the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal framework was issued at this year’s UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, and the marks were dismal. The problem is not a lack of targets, but a global financial system that pays to destroy nature and penalizes those who protect it.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Sia Kambou/AFP via Getty Images

The first report card on the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal framework was issued at this year’s UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, and the marks were dismal. The problem is not a lack of targets, but a global financial system that pays to destroy nature and penalizes those who protect it.

By Homi Kharas, Julie McCarthy and Ichiro Sato

WASHINGTON, DC—Four years ago, the United Nations Biodiversity Conference in Montreal adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, hailed at the time as the “Paris agreement for nature.” But the first assessment of the framework’s implementation, released at October’s UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) in Yerevan, makes for sobering reading. The State of Biodiversity Action report finds that while nearly 90% of countries have set targets to protect 30% of land and sea areas, restore 30% of degraded ecosystems, and halt human-caused extinctions, fewer than half of the assessed targets are on track to be met by 2030.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres called COP17 “our moment of accountability.” But while accountability is long overdue, finding a solution requires accurately diagnosing the problem. The Kunming-Montreal framework is faltering not because governments are indifferent to nature, but because global economic and financial systems reward nature’s destruction and penalize its protection. According to the UN Environment Programme, in 2023, $7.3 trillion—roughly 7% of world GDP—flowed into activities that directly harm nature. For every dollar invested in nature that year, $30 was spent destroying it.

The Kunming-Montreal framework calls for closing the biodiversity finance gap, which amounts to $700 billion annually, by reducing nature-harming subsidies by $500 billion per year and mobilizing $200 billion per year in incremental finance, including $30 billion from external official sources. Well over half of that investment is needed to implement sustainable management practices for farmland, rangeland, fisheries, and forests. The remainder is for ecosystem restoration and preservation.

The issue is bigger than market failures. As David Obura argues in our co-edited volume Nature, People, and Sustainable Development, there is a fundamental mismatch between what we value and what is needed. At best, prices capture nature’s usefulness. To reflect nature’s relational or intrinsic worth requires reframing the problem as not just conservation, which looks like a cost—land tied up and growth forgone—that rich countries foist on poor ones. Credit-ratings agencies, pointing to the risk of slower growth, then downgrade developing countries’ credit ratings.

A far better approach is to emphasize the bioeconomy’s potential, which positions protecting nature as a growth strategy. Around 55% of global GDP—equivalent to $58 trillion—already depends directly on nature. The bioeconomy, which uses biological resources in a regenerative and nature-positive way, is worth about $4 trillion today; unlocking its potential could boost its value to $30 trillion by 2050 and link producers to global supply chains that can steer them toward higher value-added activities.

The problem of underinvestment is most acute in countries with abundant natural resources but limited fiscal space, including Indonesia, Brazil, Peru, Zambia, Ecuador, the Philippines, and Mozambique. These governments often rely on extractive activities such as logging, mining, and plantation agriculture to earn foreign exchange, which tends to go toward servicing their external debt. The resulting ecological damage leaves them more exposed to floods, droughts, storms, and other climate disasters that usually lead to rating downgrades. By contrast, debt frameworks do not properly account for the benefits of building resilience to such shocks.

Creating the right incentives is especially important in commodity supply chains. For example, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana produce nearly two-thirds of the world’s cocoa supply, almost entirely on small farms. But 73–90% of households producing cocoa in these countries earn little income from it, and cannot afford the fertilizer and weed-control costs of replanting aging trees, so they push into forests where it is cheaper to plant new ones.

But with chocolate trading, processing, and manufacturing concentrated in a handful of firms, a few players can have an outsize impact on global outcomes. The European Union, which imports about 58% of the world’s cocoa beans, will begin to apply the Deforestation Regulation to large operators starting in December, making access to the European market for cocoa, coffee, and other commodities conditional on deforestation-free supply chains. But to improve compliance, some of the big traders should be encouraged to finance replanting and traceability efforts, so that smallholder farmers can meet the rules and earn more by doing so.

Protecting nature is also a security imperative, with environmental crime—illegal logging, mining, wildlife trafficking, and fishing—generating an estimated $110–280 billion per year, much of it laundered through the same channels as proceeds from narcotics and illicit finance. Instead of chasing individual loggers, enforcement and asset recovery should target chokepoints like mills, refineries, ports, traders, and financiers, while securing land rights and public finance for nature’s most effective stewards: Indigenous peoples and local communities, whose relationships with nature reflect its relational and intrinsic values.

The lesson of the State of Biodiversity Action report is that adding targets while treating nature as just another economic sector will not work. As the future of climate and nature action are once again negotiated at this month’s UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya and in discussions at the UN about the agenda to replace the Sustainable Development Goals after 2030, we must focus on changing the incentives that have stalled progress. That means framing nature as an investment, not a cost—and rewarding, not punishing, those who protect it.

Homi Kharas is a senior fellow at the Center for Sustainable Development at the Brookings Institution and co-editor of Nature, People, and Sustainable Development (Brookings, 2026).

Julie McCarthy is CEO of NatureFinance and co-editor of Nature, People, and Sustainable Development (Brookings, 2026).

Ichiro Sato is an executive senior research fellow at the JICA Ogata Sadako Research Institute for Peace and Development and co-editor of Nature, People, and Sustainable Development (Brookings, 2026).

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: Only Israel’s Arab Parties Can Restore Its Democracy
item.dc:creator: Shlomo Ben-Ami
item.description: While Israel’s recent election did not deliver the transformation for which many might have hoped, it could open the way to restoring Israeli democracy. By building a coalition with the Arab-led parties, the opposition bloc could defeat not only Benjamin Netanyahu but also the violent, racist ideology he embodies.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images

While Israel’s recent election did not deliver the transformation for which many might have hoped, it could open the way to restoring Israeli democracy. By building a coalition with the Arab-led parties, the opposition bloc could defeat not only Benjamin Netanyahu but also the violent, racist ideology he embodies.

By Shlomo Ben-Ami

TEL AVIV—Before Israel’s election, I warned that no one should pin high hopes on the outcome. Sadly, that advice has been vindicated. An electorate deeply split along tribal and cultural lines did not hold Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accountable for multiple prolonged wars, overseeing countless war crimes, and decimating Israel’s global standing. Instead, the vote delivered a deadlock.

Continues on Project Syndicate (registration required)

item.title: Making the Most of America’s Midterm Tsunami
item.dc:creator: Aziz Huq
item.description: American voters’ demand for the rule of law and democracy has helped destroy Trump’s MAGA movement. Affordability may have ranked first among their concerns, but addressing it will depend on repairing and improving democratic institutions.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: John Lazenby/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

American voters’ demand for the rule of law and democracy has helped destroy Trump’s MAGA movement. Affordability may have ranked first among their concerns, but addressing it will depend on repairing and improving democratic institutions.

By Aziz Huq

CHICAGO—Imagine, for a moment, that the US midterm elections had not delivered Democratic wins at a generational scale, but merely a trickle of flipped seats—enough, perhaps, to change control of the House of Representatives but not enough for a Senate majority. Is there any doubt that President Donald Trump would embrace such results as a good-enough validation of his often lawless and brutal administration? Would it not now be doubling down, striving to cast the polls as an imprimatur for its excesses?

item.title: AI Can Help Governments Help Citizens
item.dc:creator: Kalpana Kochhar
item.description: In developing economies, the AI debate has focused less on frontier risk and more on how to ensure that the technology actually serves people. That will require not only designing AI tools to work within government, but also investing in the state capacity required to put the technology to use.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: elenabs/Getty Images

In developing economies, the AI debate has focused less on frontier risk and more on how to ensure that the technology actually serves people. That will require not only designing AI tools to work within government, but also investing in the state capacity required to put the technology to use.

By Kalpana Kochhar

WASHINGTON, DC—Many countries are trying to do more for their citizens, albeit often with outdated systems. That means accessing government services can feel like a second job. A mother walks half a day to a clinic, only to be turned away because she needs a form from an office in another town. A farmer who qualifies for financial support gives up after being passed from queue to queue. AI, if used correctly, could help close these gaps, expanding a capable state’s reach.

For low- and middle-income countries, the stakes could not be higher: AI could be a great equalizer, or it could deepen inequality. While AI’s likely contributions to agriculture, health care, and education hold great promise, the World Bank’s World Development Report 2026 estimates that AI’s productivity benefits could be more than twice as large in advanced economies if current trends continue. The technology’s future trajectory depends on the decisions that developers, investors, and governments make today about how it is built, funded, and deployed.

As Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, explained at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in October, AI adoption depends on electricity access, digital connectivity, and workers equipped with the right skills. But after decades spent in development finance, I am convinced that access, while a legitimate concern, is not the biggest barrier. Above all, AI adoption requires building the state capacity to put these tools to use.

In advanced economies, the AI debate has largely focused on safety, security, and the threat of job displacement. But in developing economies, the more immediate question is how to ensure that AI tools actually serve people. They must work in local languages, train on local data, and be built for local realities. And they must be coupled with investment in the institutions and people closest to the problem, who understand where AI tools can deliver real benefits and can ensure that they do. Much of this essential work falls to the companies building these tools and the funders backing them.

But even the best-built tools will struggle to deliver results if governments lack the capacity to implement them. Creating that capacity requires integrating AI systems into existing programs. Consider MahaVISTAAR, a free AI advisory service that the Indian state of Maharashtra built for farmers to ask about crops, weather, and pests in their own language through an app, voice call, or chat. So far, more than 740,000 farmers have joined, with 70,000 new users signing up each month, at a cost to the government of less than 18 cents per farmer—a fraction of what it would cost to reach them in person. The tool worked because the government viewed it as a new layer of public infrastructure built on its network for advising farmers, rather than a one-off app.

On a recent visit to Pakistan, I witnessed a provincial government working to build this kind of capacity, which it views as a public good. Punjab has established a government office dedicated to AI and is collaborating with local researchers to develop public-health applications, including local-language tools that help frontline workers reach mothers with the right guidance at the right time.

AI tools intended to serve citizens must work within government, not merely be adapted to it. They must be built to run on public systems and data, adhere to the data-sharing and security protocols that policymakers have selected for their countries, and be affordable enough for governments to procure and sustain them.

In my experience, three elements are essential to building AI capacity. First, governments need leaders who can determine the best use cases for AI, alongside institutional ownership and cross-ministry coordination. An AI strategy needs a clear budget and detailed timelines, and should be backed by empowered ministries and a mechanism that makes decisions binding across agencies. This could reduce the likelihood of parallel projects, which may result in duplication and suboptimal outcomes, eroding the limited capability that already exists.

Second, countries need civil servants with enough AI expertise to commission, acquire, integrate, evaluate, and regulate these systems. That means developing talent pipelines that channel people with the necessary technical skills—distinct from general digital literacy—toward government roles. While not even wealthy countries have figured out how to meet this demand, developing countries can hardly afford to neglect it.

Third, governments must build integrated digital public infrastructure, including e-government service delivery, digital ID, payments, and a secure data exchange layer. Weak digitization and fragmented vertical systems are a direct constraint on AI performance and safety. Once that infrastructure is in place, AI can in turn help make government systems more secure—detecting fraud, cyberattacks, and anomalous patterns.

Building the tools may be the more straightforward part. Whether AI reaches that mother or that farmer will be determined less by the pace of the technology than by the choices governments make now. If policymakers get it right, AI can help a country fulfill its most basic, and most important, duty: serving its citizens effectively.

Kalpana Kochhar is Interim President of Global Policy & Advocacy at the Gates Foundation.

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: MAGA’s Midterm Defeat Won’t Change the Course of History
item.dc:creator: Slavoj Žižek
item.description: The world must not succumb to euphoria following Donald Trump’s latest defeat. If anything, his lame-duck status deprives Americans and everyone else of an excuse for avoiding hard conversations about the truly radical changes that will be needed to avert future catastrophes.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images

The world must not succumb to euphoria following Donald Trump’s latest defeat. If anything, his lame-duck status deprives Americans and everyone else of an excuse for avoiding hard conversations about the truly radical changes that will be needed to avert future catastrophes.

By Slavoj Žižek

LJUBLJANA—My duty as a philosopher is to spoil the ecstatic sense of relief that has followed the US midterm elections. Yes, at first glance, we all triumphed: not only did Donald Trump’s party suffer a spectacular defeat, but Trump even accepted his loss and promised to work with the incoming Democratic Congress. We were spared the state of emergency or canceled results that so many had feared.

Continues on Project Syndicate (registration required)

item.title: Can AI Colonialism Be Prevented?
item.dc:creator: Jayant Sinha
item.description: As the United States and China cement their technological dominance, the AI revolution threatens to reproduce the colonial dynamics of the first Industrial Revolution. To avoid digital colonization, middle powers must work together to build an open AI stack and establish common standards to govern it.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: DrAfter123/Getty Images

As the United States and China cement their technological dominance, the AI revolution threatens to reproduce the colonial dynamics of the first Industrial Revolution. To avoid digital colonization, middle powers must work together to build an open AI stack and establish common standards to govern it.

By Jayant Sinha

NEW DELHI—The world is entering the AI age with the United States and China having established clear technological dominance over all other countries. These two superpowers now control virtually every layer of the “stack”: the hardware, data systems, software, and apps that, together, compose AI. They are also investing in AI infrastructure at a pace other countries cannot match.

Continues on Project Syndicate (subscriber article)

item.title: Turning Sub-Saharan Africa’s Cities Into Job Engines
item.dc:creator: Paschal Donohoe
item.description: Cities and towns will be central to creating more and better jobs for Sub-Saharan Africa’s fast-growing population, simply because the region’s people and economic activity are increasingly concentrated there. But unlocking urbanization’s potential requires policy guidance and well-planned investment.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty Images

Cities and towns will be central to creating more and better jobs for Sub-Saharan Africa’s fast-growing population, simply because the region’s people and economic activity are increasingly concentrated there. But unlocking urbanization’s potential requires policy guidance and well-planned investment.

By Paschal Donohoe

WASHINGTON, DC—Recent visits to South Africa and Ghana brought home to me the scale of Africa’s urban development opportunity. In Johannesburg and Accra, I saw fast-growing cities, teeming with ambition, innovation, and young people looking to build better lives. Their challenges are significant, but so, too, is their potential to create jobs and drive growth.

Continues on Project Syndicate (registration required)

item.title: Why Are Indian Protesters Targeting the Electoral Commission?
item.dc:creator: Shashi Tharoor
item.description: Following a “special intensive revision” that struck 130 million voters from the electoral rolls, India’s youth have mounted large-scale protests against the Election Commission. Given the convergence of protests with the formal political opposition, the Commission is unlikely to avoid accountability for mass disenfranchisement.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Arun Sankar/AFP via Getty Images

Following a “special intensive revision” that struck 130 million voters from the electoral rolls, India’s youth have mounted large-scale protests against the Election Commission. Given the convergence of protests with the formal political opposition, the Commission is unlikely to avoid accountability for mass disenfranchisement.

By Shashi Tharoor

NEW DELHI—Following a summer of discontent, India has entered an autumn of political crisis. During a scorching June and July, a youth-led movement, backed by Rahul Gandhi’s opposition Congress party, took to the streets to demand education reform. So potent was the movement that the central government, led by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), was forced to make significant concessions, including the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. But Indians are not finished: they have now set their sights on the electoral system.
